**Tafsir of Surah al-Dhariyat**

This surah is Meccan by the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun).

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿By the scatterers scattering,﴾ ﴿and the bearers of burdens (carrying a load),﴾ ﴿and the runners running with ease,﴾ ﴿and the distributors distributing command,﴾ ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true,﴾ ﴿and indeed, the Recompense is certainly going to happen.﴾ ﴿By the sky with its folds (ḥubuk),﴾ ﴿indeed, you are in a discordant saying.﴾ ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away.﴾ ﴿Cursed are the conjecturers,﴾ ﴿who are in heedlessness, inattentive.﴾ ﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾ ﴿The Day they will be tried over the Fire.﴾ ﴿"Taste your trial. This is what you used to seek to hasten."﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿receiving what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were, before that, doers of good.﴾

God swears by these created things in order to draw attention to them, to honour them, and to indicate that they should be considered, so that whoever looks at them arrives at the oneness of God, the Exalted.

As for "al-Dhariyat" (the scatterers): it means the winds, by the consensus of those who interpret the text. It is said: "dharat al-rih wa adharat" (the wind scattered), with the same meaning. In the winds there is a lesson from their strength at times, their gentleness at other times, and their being at one time a mercy and at another a punishment, and so on. "Dharwan" (scattering) is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar).

As for "al-ḥamilat wiqran" (the bearers of a load): ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭalib, may God be pleased with him, said: they are the clouds laden with water. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, and others said: they are the ships laden with people and their goods. A group of scholars said: they are also, in addition to this, all animals that carry loads. In all of this there is a lesson. "Wiqran" is a direct object (maf'ul ṣarih).

As for "al-jariyat yusran" (the runners running with ease): ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭalib, may God be pleased with him, and others said: they are the ships on the sea. Others said: they are the clouds moving with the wind. Others said: they are the moving stars. The wording allows all of this. "Yusran" is an adjective (naʿt) of an omitted infinitive, and the adjectives of omitted infinitives return as circumstantial modifiers (aḥwal). The meaning of "yusran" is: with ease and little effort.

As for "al-muqassimat amran" (the distributors of command): they are the angels. "Amr" here is a collective noun (ism al-jins), so it is as if He, the Exalted, said: and the groups that distribute the affairs of the dominion (malakut), such as provisions, lifespans, creation in the wombs, the affairs of the winds, and other things, because all of this happens through angels who serve Him. Thus the verse includes all the angels, since they are all in different affairs. The feminine form "al-muqassimat" is used because He meant the groups.

Then Ibn al-Kiwa stood up and asked him about these (verses). He said: "The dhariyat are the winds, the hamilat are the clouds, the jariyat are the ships, and the muqassimat are the angels." Then he said to him: "Ask a question of learning, and do not ask a question of obstinacy."

This oath applies to His saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾. "Tu'adun" (you are promised) may be from al-iʿad (threatening) or from al-waʿd (promising). Whichever it is, describing it as true is correct. "Ṣadiq" (true) here is in place of a noun (badal) for "ṣidq" (truth); the active participle is placed in the position of the infinitive.

As for "al-din" (the Recompense): it means the requital. Mujahid said: it means the reckoning. The most apparent meaning of the verse is that it addresses the disbelievers, and that it is a pure threat concerning the Day of Resurrection.

Then God, the Exalted, swore by another created thing, saying: ﴿By the sky with its folds﴾. The apparent meaning of the word "al-sama'" (the sky) is that it refers to all the heavens. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs said: it is the seventh heaven. "Al-ḥubuk" (with the vowels ḥubuk, pronounced with ḍamma on both the ḥa' and the ba') means the lines that are arranged in an order within the bodies. Thus the "ḥabk" of sand and water is the lines that the blowing wind produces upon them. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Covered with dense growth of plants, which a stormy autumn wind weaves, with the bright surface of its water having folds (ḥubuk).*

In a hadith: « "Indeed, behind you is the lying, misleading one (al-Dajjal), and indeed his head behind him is ḥubuk ḥubuk" », meaning the curliness of his hair; it is its curling. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, explained the saying of God, the Exalted, ﴿By the sky with its folds﴾ by saying: "Its ḥubuk is the beauty of its creation." Ibn Jubayr said: "The ḥubuk is adornment." Al-Hasan said: "Its ḥubuk is its stars." Ibn Zayd said: "The ḥubuk is strength; ḥubikat means shuddat (it was made strong)," and he recited: "seven strong (shidad)." Ibn Jinni said: "The ḥubuk are the streaks of cloud and the like." The singular of "ḥubuk" may also be ḥabika.

Al-Hasan also, as is reported from him, recited "al-ḥibuk" with kasra on the ḥa' and ḍamma on the ba'; this is an anomalous dialect that is not well-founded. It seems he intended the kasra on both, then he imagined the reading "al-ḥabuk" with ḍamma after having kasra on the ḥa', so he put ḍamma on the ba'. This is by the mixing of dialects, and this pattern does not occur in Arabic speech. ʿIkrima recited "al-ḥubak" with ḍamma on the ḥa' and fatḥa on the ba', the plural of ḥubka. All of these are dialects, and the meaning is what we have mentioned. A "maḥbuk" horse is one of strong build that has ḥubak (curls) in places where its hair grows, and that is a sign of the excellence of its structure.

This is the saying of Qatada. It may also be an address to the disbelievers only, meaning: you are, in a kind of saying, differing in itself. A people among you say "sorcerer," a people say "soothsayer," a people say "poet," a people say "madman," and so on. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd. The pronoun in "ʿanhu" (from it): al-Hasan and Qatada said it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, or to his Book, or to his law. "Yu'fak" means "is turned away," so the meaning is: many of the disbelievers are turned away from the Book of God, the Exalted. It may also be that the pronoun returns to the saying by which whoever wants Islam is turned away, by saying of it: "It is sorcery; it is soothsaying." This is an opinion related by al-Zahrawi. It may also be that the pronoun in "ʿanhu" returns to the saying, meaning: whoever's happiness prevails is turned away from it by the grace of God, the Exalted, to Islam. This is on the basis that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, you are in a discordant saying﴾, is addressed to the disbelievers only. This is a good interpretation that does not undermine it. However, the usage of "ifk" is known to be used only for turning from good to evil. Reflect on this and you will find it always applied to those who are turned away and are blameworthy. Abu ʿAmr related from Qatada that he recited "man afaka" with fatḥa on the hamza and the fa'.

Their urging to hasten is their saying: "When is the Day of Recompense?" and other statements that imply their urging to hasten, in the manner of denial on their part.

When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and what they receive of the punishment of God, the Mighty and Majestic, He followed that with mention of the God-fearing and what they receive of bliss, to make the difference clear and to lead people to the path of guidance. "Al-jannat" (gardens) and springs are well known. The "muttaqi" (God-fearing) in the verse is unrestricted in guarding against disbelief and sins. His saying, the Exalted, "ākhidhin" (receiving) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal). Ibn Abi ʿAbla recited "ākhidhūn" with a wāw. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: the meaning is: taking in their worldly life what their Lord gave them of His commands, His prohibitions, His obligations, and His law. The state on this reading is reported (maḥkiyya), and it precedes in time their being in gardens and springs. A group of exegetes said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿receiving what their Lord has given them﴾ is: sincerely accepting the favours of God, the Exalted, which He has given them of His Paradise and His good pleasure. This state is connected in meaning to their being in the gardens. This interpretation is more preferable in my view, because the discourse is consistent with it. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿before that﴾ means: in the world. "Muḥsinin" (doers of good) means: through obedience and righteous action.

God swears by these created things in order to draw attention to them, to honour them, and to indicate that they should be considered, so that whoever looks at them arrives at the oneness of God, the Exalted.

As for "al-Dhariyat" (the scatterers): it means the winds, by the consensus of those who interpret the text. It is said: "dharat al-rih wa adharat" (the wind scattered), with the same meaning. In the winds there is a lesson from their strength at times, their gentleness at other times, and their being at one time a mercy and at another a punishment, and so on. "Dharwan" (scattering) is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar).

As for "al-ḥamilat wiqran" (the bearers of a load): ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭalib, may God be pleased with him, said: they are the clouds laden with water. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, and others said: they are the ships laden with people and their goods. A group of scholars said: they are also, in addition to this, all animals that carry loads. In all of this there is a lesson. "Wiqran" is a direct object (maf'ul ṣarih).

As for "al-jariyat yusran" (the runners running with ease): ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭalib, may God be pleased with him, and others said: they are the ships on the sea. Others said: they are the clouds moving with the wind. Others said: they are the moving stars. The wording allows all of this. "Yusran" is an adjective (naʿt) of an omitted infinitive, and the adjectives of omitted infinitives return as circumstantial modifiers (aḥwal). The meaning of "yusran" is: with ease and little effort.

As for "al-muqassimat amran" (the distributors of command): they are the angels. "Amr" here is a collective noun (ism al-jins), so it is as if He, the Exalted, said: and the groups that distribute the affairs of the dominion (malakut), such as provisions, lifespans, creation in the wombs, the affairs of the winds, and other things, because all of this happens through angels who serve Him. Thus the verse includes all the angels, since they are all in different affairs. The feminine form "al-muqassimat" is used because He meant the groups.

Abu al-Tufayl ʿAmir ibn Wathila said: ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, was on the pulpit and said: "Do not ask me about any verse of the Book of God, the Exalted, or about an established Sunnah, except that I will answer." Then Ibn al-Kiwa stood up and asked him about these (verses). He said: "The dhariyat are the winds, the hamilat are the clouds, the jariyat are the ships, and the muqassimat are the angels." Then he said to him: "Ask a question of learning, and do not ask a question of obstinacy."

This oath applies to His saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾. "Tu'adun" (you are promised) may be from al-iʿad (threatening) or from al-waʿd (promising). Whichever it is, describing it as true is correct. "Ṣadiq" (true) here is in place of a noun (badal) for "ṣidq" (truth); the active participle is placed in the position of the infinitive.

As for "al-din" (the Recompense): it means the requital. Mujahid said: it means the reckoning. The most apparent meaning of the verse is that it addresses the disbelievers, and that it is a pure threat concerning the Day of Resurrection.

Then God, the Exalted, swore by another created thing, saying: ﴿By the sky with its folds﴾. The apparent meaning of the word "al-sama'" (the sky) is that it refers to all the heavens. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs said: it is the seventh heaven. "Al-ḥubuk" (with the vowels ḥubuk, pronounced with ḍamma on both the ḥa' and the ba') means the lines that are arranged in an order within the bodies. Thus the "ḥabk" of sand and water is the lines that the blowing wind produces upon them. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Covered with dense growth of plants, which a stormy autumn wind weaves, with the bright surface of its water having folds (ḥubuk).*

The "ḥabk" of a coat of mail is the continuous lines at the place where the rings join one another. In some bird wings there are folds (ḥubuk) like this. "Ḥubuk" is also said of the curling of hair. In a hadith: « "Indeed, behind you is the lying, misleading one (al-Dajjal), and indeed his head behind him is ḥubuk ḥubuk" », meaning the curliness of his hair; it is its curling. Lines appear in woven things, such as blankets and others, at the place where the threads intersect; these are ḥubuk. It is said: "He wove the garment and perfected its ḥabk." So these are the meanings of ḥubuk in the language.

Mundhir ibn Saʿid said: the sky, in the composition of its body, is thus, having ḥubuk, because of the excellence of its creation and the perfection of its making. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, explained the saying of God, the Exalted, ﴿By the sky with its folds﴾ by saying: "Its ḥubuk is the beauty of its creation." Ibn Jubayr said: "The ḥubuk is adornment." Al-Hasan said: "Its ḥubuk is its stars." Ibn Zayd said: "The ḥubuk is strength; ḥubikat means shuddat (it was made strong)," and he recited: "seven strong (shidad)." Ibn Jinni said: "The ḥubuk are the streaks of cloud and the like." The singular of "ḥubuk" is ḥibak. It is also said of the cord with which a reed fence and the like is tied, which is elongated and made in the (spread) arrangement of the lined-up plantings: ḥibak. The singular of "ḥubuk" may also be ḥabika.

The Rajaz poet said:

*As if the weaver had covered it with a cloak, a patterned covering in its embroidery, with ḥibak.*

Most people recited "al-ḥubuk" with ḍamma on the ḥa' and the ba'. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Abu Malik al-Ghifari recited with ḍamma on the ḥa' and sukun on the ba', for lightness; this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, like "rusl" for "rusul." This is the reading of Abu Haywa and Abu al-Sammal. Al-Hasan also, and Abu Malik al-Ghifari, recited "al-ḥibik" with kasra on the ḥa' and the ba', as a dialect like "iṭil" and "ibil." Al-Hasan also recited "al-ḥibk" with kasra on the ḥa' and sukun on the ba', as they said, for lightness: "ibil" and "iṭil" with sukun on the ba' and the ṭa'. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, recited "al-ḥabak" with fatḥa on the ḥa' and the ba'. Al-Hasan also, as is reported from him, recited "al-ḥibuk" with kasra on the ḥa' and ḍamma on the ba'; this is an anomalous dialect that is not well-founded. It seems he intended the kasra on both, then he imagined the reading "al-ḥabuk" with ḍamma after having kasra on the ḥa', so he put ḍamma on the ba'. This is by the mixing of dialects, and this pattern does not occur in Arabic speech. ʿIkrima recited "al-ḥubak" with ḍamma on the ḥa' and fatḥa on the ba', the plural of ḥubka. All of these are dialects, and the meaning is what we have mentioned. A "maḥbuk" horse is one of strong build that has ḥubak (curls) in places where its hair grows, and that is a sign of the excellence of its structure.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you are in a discordant saying﴾: it may be an address to all people, believers and disbelievers, meaning: you have differed, so that some of you said, "We believe in Muhammad and his Book," and another group said, "We disbelieve." This is the saying of Qatada. It may also be an address to the disbelievers only, meaning: you are, in a kind of saying, differing in itself. A people among you say "sorcerer," a people say "soothsayer," a people say "poet," a people say "madman," and so on. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd. The pronoun in "ʿanhu" (from it): al-Hasan and Qatada said it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, or to his Book, or to his law. "Yu'fak" means "is turned away," so the meaning is: many of the disbelievers are turned away from the Book of God, the Exalted. It may also be that the pronoun returns to the saying by which whoever wants Islam is turned away, by saying of it: "It is sorcery; it is soothsaying." This is an opinion related by al-Zahrawi. It may also be that the pronoun in "ʿanhu" returns to the saying, meaning: whoever's happiness prevails is turned away from it by the grace of God, the Exalted, to Islam. This is on the basis that His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, you are in a discordant saying﴾, is addressed to the disbelievers only. This is a good interpretation that does not undermine it. However, the usage of "ifk" is known to be used only for turning from good to evil. Reflect on this and you will find it always applied to those who are turned away and are blameworthy. Abu ʿAmr related from Qatada that he recited "man afaka" with fatḥa on the hamza and the fa'.

As for His saying, the Exalted: "Cursed are the conjecturers" (qutila al-kharrasun): it is an invocation against them, as you say: "qatalahu Allah" (may God kill him), "qatalahu Allah," and "ʿaqra ḥalqa" (may he be barren, may he be cut off). Some exegetes said: its meaning is "may the conjecturers be cursed." This is an explanation that the wording does not give. "Al-kharrasu" (the conjecturer) is one who guesses and estimates with his opinion. It includes the soothsayer, the doubter, and the like, anyone who has no certainty. The reference is to the deniers of Muhammad ﷺ in every way of their methods.

"Al-ghamra" is that which covers and envelops a person, like the flood of water. The meaning is: in a flood of ignorance. "Sahun" (inattentive) means: they are oblivious that they are in a flood and oblivious of other aspects of consideration.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Recompense?"﴾: its meaning is that they say, "When is the Day of Recompense?" in the sense of denial. It is permissible that some of them accompany this with mockery and that others do not. As-Sulami and al-Aʿmash recited "iyan" with kasra on the hamza and fatḥa on the ya', lightened.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day they will be tried over the Fire﴾: al-Zajjaj said: they put "yawm" in the accusative as an adverb of time governed by an implied verb, whose estimate is: it occurs on the day they are over the Fire, or something like this. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: its accusative is due to its being built, because it is attached to something non-declinable (ghayr mutamakkin). Some grammarians said: it is in the place of the nominative as an apposition (badal) to "yawm al-Din." "Yuftanun" means: they are burned and tortured in the Fire. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrima, and everyone. From it comes the saying that a free woman (ḥurra) is called "fatin," as if the sun had burned her stones. From it is the saying of Kaʿb ibn Malik:

*Its ornaments, toward which the waist-cloth (pl. "ḥaqw") inclines, whoever sees them thinks they are burned (fatin).*

"Fatantu al-dhahab" means: I burned the gold. Since it is not burned except for the sake of testing, every test is called "fitna." They used "iftutina" with the meaning of "ikhtubira" (was tested). The "ʿala" here serves to convey the meaning of "fi" (in). In His saying, ﴿Taste your trial (fitnatakum)﴾ there is an implied element, meaning: it is said to them, "Taste your burning and your punishment." This was said by Qatada and others. "Dhawq" (tasting) is a metaphor. "Hadha" (this) refers to their burning. Their urging to hasten is their saying: "When is the Day of Recompense?" and other statements that imply their urging to hasten, in the manner of denial on their part.

When the Exalted mentioned the state of the disbelievers and what they receive of the punishment of God, the Mighty and Majestic, He followed that with mention of the God-fearing and what they receive of bliss, to make the difference clear and to lead people to the path of guidance. "Al-jannat" (gardens) and springs are well known. The "muttaqi" (God-fearing) in the verse is unrestricted in guarding against disbelief and sins. His saying, the Exalted, "ākhidhin" (receiving) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal). Ibn Abi ʿAbla recited "ākhidhūn" with a wāw. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: the meaning is: taking in their worldly life what their Lord gave them of His commands, His prohibitions, His obligations, and His law. The state on this reading is reported (maḥkiyya), and it precedes in time their being in gardens and springs. A group of exegetes said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿receiving what their Lord has given them﴾ is: sincerely accepting the favours of God, the Exalted, which He has given them of His Paradise and His good pleasure. This state is connected in meaning to their being in the gardens. This interpretation is more preferable in my view, because the discourse is consistent with it. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿before that﴾ means: in the world. "Muḥsinin" (doers of good) means: through obedience and righteous action.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 51, verse 17–26:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾ ﴿and at dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾ ﴿and in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾ ﴿and in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised﴾ ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as it is true that you speak﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honoured guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Peace, [you are] an unknown people."﴾ ﴿Then he went to his family and brought a fattened calf﴾

The meaning of His saying, ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾, is that their sleep was little because they were occupied with prayer and worship. Thus what is meant is [this of] every night. "Al-hujū'" (sleep) means sleep. Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I am not among the people of this verse," and this is a fair assessment on his part. It was said to one of the Successors (tabi'un): "God, exalted be He, has praised a man who sleeps when he is drowsy and obeys his Lord when he awakes." Anas ibn Malik interpreted this verse as meaning that they would engage in voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham said: the meaning is that they would take a portion of the night [for worship]. Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah said: Few were the nights that passed over them in which they slept through all of them. Ibn Abi Najih and Mujahid also said this, so what is meant by His saying, "of the night" (min al-layl), according to these, is "of the nights" (min al-layali). The apparent meaning of the verse, in my view, is that they would stand [in prayer] for most of their night, that is, every night. Al-Hasan said in explaining this verse: they endured the standing of the night, sleeping from it only a little.

As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the verse: al-Dahhak, in the book of al-Tabari, gave an interpretation that implies the meaning is: "They were few in number." The sentence of "kana" (was) is then complete, and he began anew with "min al-layl ma yahja'un", so "ma" is a negation particle, and "qalilan" is a good pause (waqf hasan). Some grammarians said: "ma" is redundant (za'ida), and "qalilan" is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) of "yahja'un". The majority of grammarians said: "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyya), and "qalilan" is the predicate of "kana", and the meaning is: "They used to be few in the night in their sleeping." "Al-hujū'" (sleeping) is raised by "qalilan" as its subject. According to this analysis, the saying of al-Hasan and others comes out — and it is the apparent meaning to me — that what is meant is: their sleep during the night was little.

Ibn 'Umar and al-Dahhak interpreted "yastaghfirun" (they seek forgiveness) as "yusalluna" (they pray). Al-Hasan said its meaning is: they lay claim to seeking forgiveness. The times before dawn are the occasion for seeking forgiveness. It is narrated that the gates of Paradise are opened at the dawn of every day. In the story of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾ [Yusuf: 98], [it is related] that he postponed seeking forgiveness for them (p-68) until the pre-dawn (sahar). Abu Zayd said in the book of al-Tabari: "al-sahar" is the last sixth of the night.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾. The correct view is that it is muhkam (not abrogated), and that this right is by way of recommendation (nadb), not by way of obligation (fard). "Ma'lum" is intended to mean "customary" (mut'araf). Likewise the night prayer for which they were praised is not among the obligatory duties, and most of what is obligatory happens through the performance of recommended acts. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the obligatory zakat. This is weak, because the surah is Meccan, and the obligation of zakat was in Medina. Some of the interpreters said: this was [a ruling] that was later abrogated by zakat. This is not strong, for God, Exalted and Majestic, did not legislate anything in Mecca before the Hijra concerning taking wealth.

People differed about "al-mahrum" (the deprived), in a disagreement which, in my view, is a confusion introduced by later scholars, since the meaning is one. The scholars of the early generations expressed themselves in these phrasings by way of examples, but the later scholars treated them as separate sayings. Makki counted them as eight. "Al-mahrum" is the one from whom the possible means of provision remain distant after having been near to him, so he suffers deprivation and poverty, and yet he does not ask. This is the one who has a right in the wealth of the rich, just as the beggar has a right. Al-Sha'bi said: "I am unable to know what 'al-mahrum' is." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "al-mahrum" is the one who fights [in God's cause] and has no share of wealth in Islam, so he is the one with a limited craft. Abu Qilaba said: A flood came to Yamama and carried away a man's wealth, and a man from the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: "This is al-mahrum." Zayd said: it is the one whose fruit is struck. Others said: it is the one whose livestock has died. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God be pleased with him, said: it is the dog.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

A dog may indeed be deprived at some times and in some states. Do you not see the one who eats moist earth from thirst... [the hadith]; and other sayings of this kind, which were only mentioned as examples. (p-69) It is as though he says: the one whose fruit is struck is among the deprived. The comprehensive meaning of these sayings is that he is the one who has no wealth because of a deprivation that has befallen him. Otherwise, the one whose fruit is struck but who has much wealth besides it is not included in this verse, by consensus.

After this there is an implied part of the discourse, whose supposition is: "So be like them, O people, and follow their path, for the reflection that leads to this is right. Thus, on the earth are signs for those who take heed and attain certainty." This is an indication of the subtleties of wisdom and the marvels of creation that are in the lands, the mountains, the minerals, the springs, and other things. Qatada read "ayatun" in the singular.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And in yourselves" refers to reflection on the person of the human being, for he is the most important of the created beings we have as a lesson, because of what God, blessed and exalted, has placed in him — despite being made of dust — of subtle senses, of the affair of the soul and its life and speech, the connection of this part of him with the intellect, and the form of the limbs and their readiness to benefit, carry, or assist. Ibn Zayd said: The heart is only a lump of flesh in the body of the son of Adam; God placed in it the intellect. Does anyone know what that intellect is, what its attribute is, and how it is? Al-Rummani said: the soul in particular is the thing which, if everything other than it that is not included in it were to perish, would not perish. This is an excessive depth which I do not commend. His saying, Exalted is He: "Will you not then see?" is a rebuke and a reproach.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾. Al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr said: God meant the rain and the snow. Al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: He meant destiny and decree, i.e., provision is with God, Exalted is He, who brings it however He wills; there is no lord other than Him. Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa fi al-sama' raziqukum" (And in the heaven is your Provider).

"Tu'adun" (you are promised) may be from "wa'd" (promise), and may be from "wa'id" (threat), and both are in the heaven. Al-Dahhak said: what is meant is from Paradise and Hell. Mujahid said: from good and evil. Ibn Sirin said: what is meant is the Hour. Then God, Exalted is He, swore by His own Self to the truth of this statement and this report, and He likened its certainty to speech in a human being, which is in his own view in utmost clarity, and it is not possible for there to occur in it the confusion that occurs in sight and hearing; rather speech is more free of such [confusion] than these.

The readers differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: "mithla ma" — Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr) read "mathalun" with a raised vowel (raf'), and it is narrated from al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-A'mash (with variation from them). Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, the people of Medina, and most people read "mithla" with a fatha. The reasoning for the first reading is the raf' as an adjective (na't) of "haqqun", and the adjective of an indefinite noun (nakira) is permitted with this, which has been made genitive to a definite noun, because "mithl" is common and general for many aspects, so the genitive construction does not make it definite; for when you say, "I saw the like of Zayd," you have not identified anything, since the aspects of resemblance are many. When the generality remains, the ruling of the indefinite applies to it, and so the indefinite is described by it. "Ma" is redundant and gives emphasis. The genitive of "mithl" has been built as with what is annexed to a non-declinable noun, and it is in the position of raf' as an attribute of "haqq", and it took on the construction (bina') because the noun in the genitive may give the noun in the construct state some of its attributes, such as the feminine gender in the saying of the poet:

...... "shariqat sadr al-qanah" ......

and such as definiteness in "ghulam Zayd", and so on. "Mithl" then runs in the manner of "'adhab yawmi'idhin" according to the reading of those who open the mim, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"'ala hina 'atabtu al-mashib 'ala al-sibā" ......

(p-71) And from it is the saying of another:

"Lam yamna' al-shurb minha ghayru an hatafat" ......

So "ghayr" is the subject, but he gave it a fatha.

The second aspect, which is the saying of al-Mazini, is that "mithl" was built because it became one thing together with "ma", and it occurs on this basis in the pattern of "waymama" and "aynama". From it is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"Alā hayyama mimma laqītu wa hayyama / wa waykun liman lam yadri ma hunna waykama"

(p-72) Were it not for the construction, it would be necessary for it to be tanwin-ed. Likewise is the saying of the poet:

"...... fa-akrim bina khalan wa akrim bina ibnama"

The third aspect is that "mithl" be put in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying, Exalted is He: "la-haqqun", and this is a hal from an indefinite noun, and there is disagreement about it, but al-Jarmi permitted it. As for others, they consider it a hal from the pronoun mentioned in "la-haqqun" in His saying, Exalted is He, because the sense is "truly it is", and in this there is consideration.

"Al-nutq" in this verse is speech by letters and sounds in the arrangement of meanings. It is narrated that one of the eloquent Arabs heard this verse and said: "Who has made the noble one need to swear?" The anecdote occurs in the book of al-Tha'labi, and "Subul al-Khayrat" completes it on the authority of al-Asma'i. It is also narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "May God fight a people to whom their Lord swore by His own Self, and they did not believe Him." Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that (p-73) the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If any of you were to flee from his provision, it would follow him just as death follows him." And the hadiths and poetry concerning provision are numerous.

His saying: "Has there reached you" is an affirmation to gather the attention of the one addressed. This is like when you begin to speak to a person about something strange and you confirm: "Did he hear it from you or not?" It is as if you demand from him that he say "No," and you invite him to ask for the narration. "Dayf" is a generic noun (ism jins) which applies to the singular and the plural. It is narrated that the guests of Abraham, peace be upon him, were Gabriel, Michael, and Israfil, along with followers of theirs among the angels, peace be upon them. God made them "honoured" either because they are so in His sight, and this is the saying of al-Hasan, or because Abraham, peace be upon him, honoured them and served them, he and Sarah, and slaughtered the calf for them. It was also said: because he raised their seats. "Salaman" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar); it is as if they said: "We greet with a greeting," or "I greet with a greeting." It is also possible that "qalu" governs it, by making "salaman" equivalent to "qawlan", so the meaning then would be that they said a greeting and a speech, meaning "peace." This is the saying of Mujahid. "Salamun" is in the nominative as the predicate of an inchoative, that is, "my affair is peace," or "peace is due to you," or it is an inchoative with the predicate omitted, as if he said: "Peace be upon you." Abraham, peace be upon him, responded with a better greeting, because their saying was a supplication, and his saying was an obligation that had been accomplished for them. Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakha'i, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha, and Ibn Jubayr read "qala silmun" with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam, and the meaning is: "We are peace," or "You are peace." His saying, Exalted is He: "qawmun munkarun" means: "We do not recognize them, and we have no acquaintance with them." This also is on the supposition: "You are an unknown people." Abu al-'Aliya said: he disapproved of their greeting in that land and at that time.

"Raagha" means: he went away in the midst of his conversation, concealing his departure, hurrying as if he did not intend to leave them; he went to a side of his house hurriedly and returned immediately. This is a likening to the well-known "rawagan" (turning aside stealthily), because the one who turns aside gives the impression that he has not moved. "Al-'ijl" is the calf which he roasted for them. It is enough to know that (p-74) he, peace be upon him, established for hospitality endowments which the nations, with their differing religions and races, continue to spend.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 51, verse 17–26:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾ ﴿and at dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾ ﴿and in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾ ﴿and in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised﴾ ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as it is true that you speak﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honoured guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Peace, [you are] an unknown people."﴾ ﴿Then he went to his family and brought a fattened calf﴾

The meaning of His saying, ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾, is that their sleep was little because they were occupied with prayer and worship. Thus what is meant is [this of] every night. "Al-hujū'" (sleep) means sleep. Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I am not among the people of this verse," and this is a fair assessment on his part. It was said to one of the Successors (tabi'un): "God, exalted be He, has praised a man who sleeps when he is drowsy and obeys his Lord when he awakes." Anas ibn Malik interpreted this verse as meaning that they would engage in voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham said: the meaning is that they would take a portion of the night [for worship]. Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah said: Few were the nights that passed over them in which they slept through all of them. Ibn Abi Najih and Mujahid also said this, so what is meant by His saying, "of the night" (min al-layl), according to these, is "of the nights" (min al-layali). The apparent meaning of the verse, in my view, is that they would stand [in prayer] for most of their night, that is, every night. Al-Hasan said in explaining this verse: they endured the standing of the night, sleeping from it only a little.

As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the verse: al-Dahhak, in the book of al-Tabari, gave an interpretation that implies the meaning is: "They were few in number." The sentence of "kana" (was) is then complete, and he began anew with "min al-layl ma yahja'un", so "ma" is a negation particle, and "qalilan" is a good pause (waqf hasan). Some grammarians said: "ma" is redundant (za'ida), and "qalilan" is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) of "yahja'un". The majority of grammarians said: "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyya), and "qalilan" is the predicate of "kana", and the meaning is: "They used to be few in the night in their sleeping." "Al-hujū'" (sleeping) is raised by "qalilan" as its subject. According to this analysis, the saying of al-Hasan and others comes out — and it is the apparent meaning to me — that what is meant is: their sleep during the night was little.

Ibn 'Umar and al-Dahhak interpreted "yastaghfirun" (they seek forgiveness) as "yusalluna" (they pray). Al-Hasan said its meaning is: they lay claim to seeking forgiveness. The times before dawn are the occasion for seeking forgiveness. It is narrated that the gates of Paradise are opened at the dawn of every day. In the story of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾ [Yusuf: 98], [it is related] that he postponed seeking forgiveness for them (p-68) until the pre-dawn (sahar). Abu Zayd said in the book of al-Tabari: "al-sahar" is the last sixth of the night.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾. The correct view is that it is muhkam (not abrogated), and that this right is by way of recommendation (nadb), not by way of obligation (fard). "Ma'lum" is intended to mean "customary" (mut'araf). Likewise the night prayer for which they were praised is not among the obligatory duties, and most of what is obligatory happens through the performance of recommended acts. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the obligatory zakat. This is weak, because the surah is Meccan, and the obligation of zakat was in Medina. Some of the interpreters said: this was [a ruling] that was later abrogated by zakat. This is not strong, for God, Exalted and Majestic, did not legislate anything in Mecca before the Hijra concerning taking wealth.

People differed about "al-mahrum" (the deprived), in a disagreement which, in my view, is a confusion introduced by later scholars, since the meaning is one. The scholars of the early generations expressed themselves in these phrasings by way of examples, but the later scholars treated them as separate sayings. Makki counted them as eight. "Al-mahrum" is the one from whom the possible means of provision remain distant after having been near to him, so he suffers deprivation and poverty, and yet he does not ask. This is the one who has a right in the wealth of the rich, just as the beggar has a right. Al-Sha'bi said: "I am unable to know what 'al-mahrum' is." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "al-mahrum" is the one who fights [in God's cause] and has no share of wealth in Islam, so he is the one with a limited craft. Others said: it is the one whose livestock has died. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God be pleased with him, said: it is the dog.

[the hadith]; and other sayings of this kind, which were only mentioned as examples. (p-69) It is as though he says: the one whose fruit is struck is among the deprived. The comprehensive meaning of these sayings is that he is the one who has no wealth because of a deprivation that has befallen him. Otherwise, the one whose fruit is struck but who has much wealth besides it is not included in this verse, by consensus.

After this there is an implied part of the discourse, whose supposition is: "So be like them, O people, and follow their path, for the reflection that leads to this is right. Thus, on the earth are signs for those who take heed and attain certainty." This is an indication of the subtleties of wisdom and the marvels of creation that are in the lands, the mountains, the minerals, the springs, and other things. Qatada read "ayatun" in the singular.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And in yourselves" refers to reflection on the person of the human being, for he is the most important of the created beings we have as a lesson, because of what God, blessed and exalted, has placed in him — despite being made of dust — of subtle senses, of the affair of the soul and its life and speech, the connection of this part of him with the intellect, and the form of the limbs and their readiness to benefit, carry, or assist. Ibn Zayd said: The heart is only a lump of flesh in the body of the son of Adam; God placed in it the intellect. Does anyone know what that intellect is, what its attribute is, and how it is? Al-Rummani said: the soul in particular is the thing which, if everything other than it that is not included in it were to perish, would not perish. This is an excessive depth which I do not commend. Al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: He meant destiny and decree, i.e., provision is with God, Exalted is He, who brings it however He wills; there is no lord other than Him. Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa fi al-sama' raziqukum" (And in the heaven is your Provider).

Mujahid said: from good and evil. Ibn Sirin said: what is meant is the Hour. ...... "shariqat sadr al-qanah" ......

"'ala hina 'atabtu al-mashib 'ala al-sibā" ......

"Alā hayyama mimma laqītu wa hayyama / wa waykun liman lam yadri ma hunna waykama"

Some of the interpreters said: this was [a ruling] that was later abrogated by zakat. This is not strong, for God, Exalted and Majestic, did not legislate anything in Mecca before the Hijra concerning taking wealth.

People differed about "al-mahrum" (the deprived), in a disagreement which, in my view, is a confusion introduced by later scholars, since the meaning is one. The scholars of the early generations expressed themselves in these phrasings by way of examples, but the later scholars treated them as separate sayings. Makki counted them as eight. His saying: "Has there reached you" is an affirmation to gather the attention of the one addressed. This is like when you begin to speak to a person about something strange and you confirm: "Did he hear it from you or not?" It is as if you demand from him that he say "No," and you invite him to ask for the narration. "Dayf" is a generic noun (ism jins) which applies to the singular and the plural. It is narrated that the guests of Abraham, peace be upon him, were Gabriel, Michael, and Israfil, along with followers of theirs among the angels, peace be upon them. God made them "honoured" either because they are so in His sight, and this is the saying of al-Hasan, or because Abraham, peace be upon him, honoured them and served them, he and Sarah, and slaughtered the calf for them. It was also said: because he raised their seats. "Salaman" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar); it is as if they said: "We greet with a greeting," or "I greet with a greeting." It is also possible that "qalu" governs it, by making "salaman" equivalent to "qawlan", so the meaning then would be that they said a greeting and a speech, meaning "peace." This is the saying of Mujahid. "Salamun" is in the nominative as the predicate of an inchoative, that is, "my affair is peace," or "peace is due to you," or it is an inchoative with the predicate omitted, as if he said: "Peace be upon you." Abraham, peace be upon him, responded with a better greeting, because their saying was a supplication, and his saying was an obligation that had been accomplished for them. Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakha'i, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha, and Ibn Jubayr read "qala silmun" with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam, and the meaning is: "We are peace," or "You are peace." His saying, Exalted is He: "qawmun munkarun" means: "We do not recognize them, and we have no acquaintance with them." This also is on the supposition: "You are an unknown people." Abu al-'Aliya said: he disapproved of their greeting in that land and at that time.

"Raagha" means: he went away in the midst of his conversation, concealing his departure, hurrying as if he did not intend to leave them; he went to a side of his house hurriedly and returned immediately. This is a likening to the well-known "rawagan" (turning aside stealthily), because the one who turns aside gives the impression that he has not moved. "Al-'ijl" is the calf which he roasted for them. It is enough to know that (p-74) he, peace be upon him, established for hospitality endowments which the nations, with their differing religions and races, continue to spend.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 51, verse 17–26:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾ ﴿and at dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾ ﴿and in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ ﴿And on the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾ ﴿and in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ ﴿And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised﴾ ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth, just as it is true that you speak﴾ ﴿Has there reached you the story of Abraham's honoured guests?﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Peace, [you are] an unknown people."﴾ ﴿Then he went to his family and brought a fattened calf﴾

The meaning of His saying, ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾, is that their sleep was little because they were occupied with prayer and worship. Thus what is meant is [this of] every night. "Al-hujū'" (sleep) means sleep. Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays said: "I am not among the people of this verse," and this is a fair assessment on his part. It was said to one of the Successors (tabi'un): "God, exalted be He, has praised a man who sleeps when he is drowsy and obeys his Lord when he awakes." Anas ibn Malik interpreted this verse as meaning that they would engage in voluntary prayer between Maghrib and 'Isha'. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham said: the meaning is that they would take a portion of the night [for worship]. Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah said: Few were the nights that passed over them in which they slept through all of them. Ibn Abi Najih and Mujahid also said this, so what is meant by His saying, "of the night" (min al-layl), according to these, is "of the nights" (min al-layali). The apparent meaning of the verse, in my view, is that they would stand [in prayer] for most of their night, that is, every night. Al-Hasan said in explaining this verse: they endured the standing of the night, sleeping from it only a little.

As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the verse: al-Dahhak, in the book of al-Tabari, gave an interpretation that implies the meaning is: "They were few in number." The sentence of "kana" (was) is then complete, and he began anew with "min al-layl ma yahja'un", so "ma" is a negation particle, and "qalilan" is a good pause (waqf hasan). Some grammarians said: "ma" is redundant (za'ida), and "qalilan" is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) of "yahja'un". The majority of grammarians said: "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyya), and "qalilan" is the predicate of "kana", and the meaning is: "They used to be few in the night in their sleeping." "Al-hujū'" (sleeping) is raised by "qalilan" as its subject. According to this analysis, the saying of al-Hasan and others comes out — and it is the apparent meaning to me — that what is meant is: their sleep during the night was little.

Ibn 'Umar and al-Dahhak interpreted "yastaghfirun" (they seek forgiveness) as "yusalluna" (they pray). Al-Hasan said its meaning is: they lay claim to seeking forgiveness. The times before dawn are the occasion for seeking forgiveness. It is narrated that the gates of Paradise are opened at the dawn of every day. In the story of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾ [Yusuf: 98], [it is related] that he postponed seeking forgiveness for them (p-68) until the pre-dawn (sahar). Abu Zayd said in the book of al-Tabari: "al-sahar" is the last sixth of the night.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾. The correct view is that it is muhkam (not abrogated), and that this right is by way of recommendation (nadb), not by way of obligation (fard). "Ma'lum" is intended to mean "customary" (mut'araf). Likewise the night prayer for which they were praised is not among the obligatory duties, and most of what is obligatory happens through the performance of recommended acts. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the obligatory zakat. This is weak, because the surah is Meccan, and the obligation of zakat was in Medina. Some of the interpreters said: this was [a ruling] that was later abrogated by zakat. This is not strong, for God, Exalted and Majestic, did not legislate anything in Mecca before the Hijra concerning taking wealth.

People differed about "al-mahrum" (the deprived), in a disagreement which, in my view, is a confusion introduced by later scholars, since the meaning is one. The scholars of the early generations expressed themselves in these phrasings by way of examples, but the later scholars treated them as separate sayings. Makki counted them as eight. "Al-mahrum" is the one from whom the possible means of provision remain distant after having been near to him, so he suffers deprivation and poverty, and yet he does not ask. This is the one who has a right in the wealth of the rich, just as the beggar has a right. Al-Sha'bi said: "I am unable to know what 'al-mahrum' is." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "al-mahrum" is the one who fights [in God's cause] and has no share of wealth in Islam, so he is the one with a limited craft. Abu Qilaba said: A flood came to Yamama and carried away a man's wealth, and a man from the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: "This is al-mahrum." Zayd said: it is the one whose fruit is struck. Others said: it is the one whose livestock has died. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God be pleased with him, said: it is the dog.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

A dog may indeed be deprived at some times and in some states. Do you not see the one who eats moist earth from thirst... [the hadith]; and other sayings of this kind, which were only mentioned as examples. (p-69) It is as though he says: the one whose fruit is struck is among the deprived. The comprehensive meaning of these sayings is that he is the one who has no wealth because of a deprivation that has befallen him. Otherwise, the one whose fruit is struck but who has much wealth besides it is not included in this verse, by consensus.

After this there is an implied part of the discourse, whose supposition is: "So be like them, O people, and follow their path, for the reflection that leads to this is right. Thus, on the earth are signs for those who take heed and attain certainty." This is an indication of the subtleties of wisdom and the marvels of creation that are in the lands, the mountains, the minerals, the springs, and other things. Qatada read "ayatun" in the singular.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And in yourselves" refers to reflection on the person of the human being, for he is the most important of the created beings we have as a lesson, because of what God, blessed and exalted, has placed in him — despite being made of dust — of subtle senses, of the affair of the soul and its life and speech, the connection of this part of him with the intellect, and the form of the limbs and their readiness to benefit, carry, or assist. Ibn Zayd said: The heart is only a lump of flesh in the body of the son of Adam; God placed in it the intellect. Does anyone know what that intellect is, what its attribute is, and how it is? Al-Rummani said: the soul in particular is the thing which, if everything other than it that is not included in it were to perish, would not perish. This is an excessive depth which I do not commend. His saying, Exalted is He: "Will you not then see?" is a rebuke and a reproach.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾. Al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr said: God meant the rain and the snow. Al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: He meant destiny and decree, i.e., provision is with God, Exalted is He, who brings it however He wills; there is no lord other than Him. Ibn Muhaysin read: "wa fi al-sama' raziqukum" (And in the heaven is your Provider).

"Tu'adun" (you are promised) may be from "wa'd" (promise), and may be from "wa'id" (threat), and both are in the heaven. Al-Dahhak said: what is meant is from Paradise and Hell. Mujahid said: from good and evil. Ibn Sirin said: what is meant is the Hour. Then God, Exalted is He, swore by His own Self to the truth of this statement and this report, and He likened its certainty to speech in a human being, which is in his own view in utmost clarity, and it is not possible for there to occur in it the confusion that occurs in sight and hearing; rather speech is more free of such [confusion] than these.

The readers differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: "mithla ma" — Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr) read "mathalun" with a raised vowel (raf'), and it is narrated from al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-A'mash (with variation from them). Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far, the people of Medina, and most people read "mithla" with a fatha. The reasoning for the first reading is the raf' as an adjective (na't) of "haqqun", and the adjective of an indefinite noun (nakira) is permitted with this, which has been made genitive to a definite noun, because "mithl" is common and general for many aspects, so the genitive construction does not make it definite; for when you say, "I saw the like of Zayd," you have not identified anything, since the aspects of resemblance are many. When the generality remains, the ruling of the indefinite applies to it, and so the indefinite is described by it. "Ma" is redundant and gives emphasis. The genitive of "mithl" has been built as with what is annexed to a non-declinable noun, and it is in the position of raf' as an attribute of "haqq", and it took on the construction (bina') because the noun in the genitive may give the noun in the construct state some of its attributes, such as the feminine gender in the saying of the poet:

...... "shariqat sadr al-qanah" ......

and such as definiteness in "ghulam Zayd", and so on. "Mithl" then runs in the manner of "'adhab yawmi'idhin" according to the reading of those who open the mim, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"'ala hina 'atabtu al-mashib 'ala al-sibā" ......

(p-71) And from it is the saying of another:

"Lam yamna' al-shurb minha ghayru an hatafat" ......

So "ghayr" is the subject, but he gave it a fatha.

The second aspect, which is the saying of al-Mazini, is that "mithl" was built because it became one thing together with "ma", and it occurs on this basis in the pattern of "waymama" and "aynama". From it is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"Alā hayyama mimma laqītu wa hayyama / wa waykun liman lam yadri ma hunna waykama"

(p-72) Were it not for the construction, it would be necessary for it to be tanwin-ed. Likewise is the saying of the poet:

"...... fa-akrim bina khalan wa akrim bina ibnama"

The third aspect is that "mithl" be put in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying, Exalted is He: "la-haqqun", and this is a hal from an indefinite noun, and there is disagreement about it, but al-Jarmi permitted it. As for others, they consider it a hal from the pronoun mentioned in "la-haqqun" in His saying, Exalted is He, because the sense is "truly it is", and in this there is consideration.

"Al-nutq" in this verse is speech by letters and sounds in the arrangement of meanings. It is narrated that one of the eloquent Arabs heard this verse and said: "Who has made the noble one need to swear?" The anecdote occurs in the book of al-Tha'labi, and "Subul al-Khayrat" completes it on the authority of al-Asma'i. It is also narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "May God fight a people to whom their Lord swore by His own Self, and they did not believe Him." **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 51, verses 27–36:**

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿So he brought it to them and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿Then he sensed fear of them. They said, "Do not fear," and gave him good tidings of a knowing boy.﴾ ﴿Then his wife came forward in a cry, and she struck her face and said, "An old, barren woman!"﴾ ﴿They said, "Thus said your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ ﴿So We brought out those who were in it of the believers,﴾ ﴿but We found not in it except one house of the Muslims.﴾

The meaning: "So he brought it to them, and they refrained from it, so he said, 'Will you not eat?'" It is related in a hadith: "They said to him, 'We do not eat except what we have paid its price for.' Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said to them, 'I do not permit it to you except for a price.' They said, 'And what is that?' He said, 'That you mention the name of Allah Most High at the beginning, and praise Him at the end of eating.' Then some of them said to others, 'Truly, He took him as a close friend (khalil).'" When they persisted in not eating, he sensed fear of them. Al-wajs (sensing fear) is the self's inner perception and apprehensions regarding caution. The reason is that a guest's eating is a sign of security and an indication of the host's ease, and food creates a sacred bond and obligation, whereas refusing it creates estrangement. So Ibrahim (peace be upon him) feared that their refusal to eat his food was only because they intended some evil. They said to him, "Do not fear," and made him know that they were angels. They gave good tidings to him and to Sarah with him of a knowing boy, meaning one who will be knowing in the state of his obligation and acquisition of knowledge, that is, he will become knowing. "'Alim" (knowing) is an intensive form. Most people hold that the boy here is Ishaq, son of Sarah (peace be upon him), whose tidings are mentioned in more than one place. Mujahid said, "This boy is Isma'il (peace be upon him)." The first view is more likely, and the second is an error. It is related that he recognized that they were angels by inference from their giving him good tidings of the unseen.

As for His saying, "Then his wife came forward," it may mean that she drew near to them from one side of the house, or this "coming forward" may be like saying, "So-and-so came forward to insult me," or "to do such-and-such," when he earnestly pursued that and engaged in it. Al-ṣurra (a cry) is a shout. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sufyan, and al-Dahhak explained it thus, and it refers to one who is distressed and cries out. Qatada said its meaning is "with a wail." Al-Tabari said: some said she said, "Awwah!" with a cry and amazement. Al-Nahhas said: it was also said, "in (p. 75) a cry," meaning among a group of women hastening to look at the angels. His saying, "and struck her face," means she hit her face. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, "She slapped," and this is what one does when a matter overwhelms him. Sufyan, al-Suddi, and Mujahid said she struck her face with her palms, and this practice is still used among people today. Her saying, "An old, barren woman," may be understood as: "I am an old, barren woman, so how shall I bear a child?" or it may be understood as: "An old, barren woman, can she bear a child?" Al-Tabari estimated it as: "Shall an old, barren woman bear?" It is related that she had never borne a child at all. Al-"aqim (barren) refers to a woman who does not bear, and to a wind that does not fertilize trees, so there is no blessing in it.

As for their saying, ﴿Thus said your Lord﴾, meaning: as Our word that We have told you about, your Lord has said it will be. Al-Hakim (the All-Wise) is the one possessing wisdom, and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) means knowing of benefits and other known things.

Then Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said to the angels, "What is your business?" Al-khatb is an undetermined matter. It was said that it is generally used to express hardships and adversities, until people said, "The calamities of the age (khuṭūb al-zamān)," and other such expressions. It is as if he were saying, "What is this great calamity for which you have come?" Then they informed him that they had been sent to Sodom, the town of Lut (peace be upon him), to destroy its disbelieving, disobedient, and criminal people. Al-mujrim (criminal) is one who commits crimes, which are the attributes of sins, such as disbelief and the like; its singular is jarimah. Their saying, "to send upon them," means: to destroy them with these stones. When "arsala" (to send) is connected with "'ala" (upon), it carries the sense of intensified direct action and punishment. When it is connected with "ila" (to), it is lighter. Examine this and you will find it consistent. His saying, ﴿stones of clay﴾, is an explanation that departs from the usual stones of hail, which are made of water. It is related that it was clay baked in the fire of Hell until it became stone like baked brick. Musawwamah (marked) is an adjective of "stones." It was also said its meaning is "left unrestrained" (matrukah); its marking is from destruction and striking. It was also said its meaning is "distinguished by its sign from the sky," and al-sawmā means sign. That is, they are not stones of this world. Al-Zahrawi and al-Rummani said: it was said that the meaning is that upon each stone was the name of the one it was to strike. Al-Rummani said: it was also said that upon them were things like seal-rings. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: their marking, if the stones are black, has white spots, and if white, has black spots. It may also be that the meaning is that they were all known to your Lord for this purpose, marked for Him, a sign specific to Him. Al-musrif (the transgressor) is (p. 76) one who exceeds the proper limit. If it comes in a matching construction, it refers to the furthest extremes of disbelief and whatever is below them.

Then Allah Most High informed that by His command He brought out those in the town of Lut who were believers, delivering them. He returned the pronoun to the town without previously mentioning it explicitly, because its affair was well known, and because the criminal people are known to be in a town necessarily. The exegetes said: there is no difference between mentioning the believers first or later; they are two attributes. He mentioned them first by one of them and then last by the second. Al-Rummani said: the verse indicates that faith is Islam.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It appears to me that there is an added meaning which makes it good to put faith first. That is, He mentioned it together with bringing them out of the town, as if He, Most High, were saying: We commanded the bringing out of every believer, and did not require of him that he be an active doer of acts of obedience, but only belief in Allah Most High alone. Then, when He mentioned the state of the monotheists, He mentioned them by the attribute they had, which is complete belief and deeds. The house of the Muslims is the house of Lut (peace be upon him), who was with his two daughters. It was also said: and his daughter. In the book of al-Tha'labi it is said: it was said that Lut and his household numbered thirteen, and his wife perished among those who perished. This entire story is mentioned as an example for Quraysh, meaning that if they disbelieve, there will befall them the like of what befell those mentioned.

Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals,﴾ ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ ﴿marked by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ ﴿So We brought out those who were in it of the believers,﴾ ﴿but We found not in it except one house of the Muslims.﴾

The meaning: "So he brought it to them, and they refrained from it, so he said, 'Will you not eat?'" It is related in a hadith: "They said to him, 'We do not eat except what we have paid its price for.' Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said to them, 'I do not permit it to you except for a price.' They said, 'And what is that?' He said, 'That you mention the name of Allah Most High at the beginning, and praise Him at the end of eating.' Then some of them said to others, 'Truly, He took him as a close friend (khalil).'" When they persisted in not eating, he sensed fear of them. Al-wajs (sensing fear) is the self's inner perception and apprehensions regarding caution. The reason is that a guest's eating is a sign of security and an indication of the host's ease, and food creates a sacred bond and obligation, whereas refusing it creates estrangement. So Ibrahim (peace be upon him) feared that their refusal to eat his food was only because they intended some evil. They said to him, "Do not fear," and made him know that they were angels. They gave good tidings to him and to Sarah with him of a knowing boy, meaning one who will be knowing in the state of his obligation and acquisition of knowledge, that is, he will become knowing. "'Alim" (knowing) is an intensive form. Most people hold that the boy here is Ishaq, son of Sarah (peace be upon him), whose tidings are mentioned in more than one place. Mujahid said, "This boy is Isma'il (peace be upon him)." The first view is more likely, and the second is an error. It is related that he recognized that they were angels by inference from their giving him good tidings of the unseen.

As for His saying, "Then his wife came forward," it may mean that she drew near to them from one side of the house, or this "coming forward" may be like saying, "So-and-so came forward to insult me," or "to do such-and-such," when he earnestly pursued that and engaged in it. Al-ṣurra (a cry) is a shout. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sufyan, and al-Dahhak explained it thus, and it refers to one who is distressed and cries out. Qatada said its meaning is "with a wail." Al-Tabari said: some said she said, "Awwah!" with a cry and amazement. Al-Nahhas said: it was also said, "in (p. 75) a cry," meaning among a group of women hastening to look at the angels. His saying, "and struck her face," means she hit her face. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, "She slapped," and this is what one does when a matter overwhelms him. Sufyan, al-Suddi, and Mujahid said she struck her face with her palms, and this practice is still used among people today. Her saying, "An old, barren woman," may be understood as: "I am an old, barren woman, so how shall I bear a child?" or it may be understood as: "An old, barren woman, can she bear a child?" Al-Tabari estimated it as: "Shall an old, barren woman bear?" It is related that she had never borne a child at all. Al-"aqim (barren) refers to a woman who does not bear, and to a wind that does not fertilize trees, so there is no blessing in it.

As for their saying, ﴿Thus said your Lord﴾, meaning: as Our word that We have told you about, your Lord has said it will be. Al-Hakim (the All-Wise) is the one possessing wisdom, and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) means knowing of benefits and other known things.

Then Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said to the angels, "What is your business?" Al-khatb is an undetermined matter. It was said that it is generally used to express hardships and adversities, until people said, "The calamities of the age (khuṭūb al-zamān)," and other such expressions. It is as if he were saying, "What is this great calamity for which you have come?" Then they informed him that they had been sent to Sodom, the town of Lut (peace be upon him), to destroy its disbelieving, disobedient, and criminal people. Al-mujrim (criminal) is one who commits crimes, which are the attributes of sins, such as disbelief and the like; its singular is jarimah. Their saying, "to send upon them," means: to destroy them with these stones. When "arsala" (to send) is connected with "'ala" (upon), it carries the sense of intensified direct action and punishment. When it is connected with "ila" (to), it is lighter. Examine this and you will find it consistent. His saying, ﴿stones of clay﴾, is an explanation that departs from the usual stones of hail, which are made of water. It is related that it was clay baked in the fire of Hell until it became stone like baked brick. Musawwamah (marked) is an adjective of "stones." It was also said its meaning is "left unrestrained" (matrukah); its marking is from destruction and striking. It was also said its meaning is "distinguished by its sign from the sky," and al-sawmā means sign. That is, they are not stones of this world. Al-Zahrawi and al-Rummani said: it was said that the meaning is that upon each stone was the name of the one it was to strike. Al-Rummani said: it was also said that upon them were things like seal-rings. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: their marking, if the stones are black, has white spots, and if white, has black spots. It may also be that the meaning is that they were all known to your Lord for this purpose, marked for Him, a sign specific to Him. Al-musrif (the transgressor) is (p. 76) one who exceeds the proper limit. If it comes in a matching construction, it refers to the furthest extremes of disbelief and whatever is below them.

Then Allah Most High informed that by His command He brought out those in the town of Lut who were believers, delivering them. He returned the pronoun to the town without previously mentioning it explicitly, because its affair was well known, and because the criminal people are known to be in a town necessarily. The exegetes said: there is no difference between mentioning the believers first or later; they are two attributes. He mentioned them first by one of them and then last by the second. Al-Rummani said: the verse indicates that faith is Islam.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It appears to me that there is an added meaning which makes it good to put faith first. That is, He mentioned it together with bringing them out of the town, as if He, Most High, were saying: We commanded the bringing out of every believer, and did not require of him that he be an active doer of acts of obedience, but only belief in Allah Most High alone. Then, when He mentioned the state of the monotheists, He mentioned them by the attribute they had, which is complete belief and deeds. The house of the Muslims is the house of Lut (peace be upon him), who was with his two daughters. It was also said: and his daughter. In the book of al-Tha'labi it is said: it was said that Lut and his household numbered thirteen, and his wife perished among those who perished. This entire story is mentioned as an example for Quraysh, meaning that if they disbelieve, there will befall them the like of what befell those mentioned.

﴿And We left in it a sign for those who fear the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And in Moses, when We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority.﴾ ﴿But he turned away with his power and said, "A sorcerer or a madman."﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy.﴾ ﴿And in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind.﴾ ﴿It left nothing it came upon without making it like crumbled dust.﴾ ﴿And in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾ ﴿But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on.﴾

The meaning: We left in the aforementioned town, which is Sodom (Sadum), a lasting trace of punishment, its mention never perishing. It is therefore a sign (āyah), i.e. an indication, of the power of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, and of His retribution against the disbelievers. It is also possible that the meaning is: "We left [a sign] in its matter," as He said: ﴿There were certainly signs in Joseph and his brothers for those who ask.﴾ [Yusuf: 7]. Ibn Jurayj said: He left in it stones piled up, very many. And "those who fear the punishment" are those who know Allah, may He be exalted.

His saying, "And in Moses," may be a conjunction with His saying "in it," meaning: "And We left in Moses and his story a trace also, which is a sign." It may also be a conjunction with His earlier saying: ﴿And in the earth are signs for the certain.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 20]. Pharaoh is the ruler of Egypt. "Sultan" in this verse means proof. "Tawalla" means he turned away and withdrew from the command of Allah, may He be exalted. "Rukn" means his authority, his soldiers, and the severity of his affairs, which is the matter on which Pharaoh leaned and relied in his hardships. Ibn Zayd said: "with his rukn" means with his hosts. Qatadah said: with his people. Pharaoh's saying about Moses, peace be upon him, "A sorcerer or a madman," is a division of conjecture, as though Moses, peace be upon him, must be one of these two. Abu 'Ubayda said: "aw" here means "wa" (and), and he cited the verse of Jarir:

"Did you equate with them the horsemen of Tha'laba, or Riyah, or Tuhayya and al-Khishab?"

Al-Khishab are houses among the Banu Tamim. Abu 'Ubayda's view is weak, and there is no call for it in this place. "And We cast them" means We threw them away. "Al-yamm" means the sea. In the Mushaf (codex) of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "fa-nabadhnahu" (singular). "Al-mulim" is one who has committed sins or the like for which he is blamed. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"......................... And whoever forsakes his brother has indeed done wrong."

His saying, "And in 'Ad," is joined to His saying, "And in Moses." 'Ad is the tribe of the Prophet Hud, peace and blessings be upon him. "Al-'aqim" means that in which there is no blessing: it neither fertilizes trees nor drives rain. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: it was the south wind. It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was a nakba (a wind between two directions). In my view this is not authentically from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, because it contradicts the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I was made victorious by the east wind (al-saba), and 'Ad was destroyed by the west wind (al-dabur)." "Tadhar" means it leaves. His saying, ﴿from a thing it came upon﴾, means from what Allah, may He be exalted, permitted it to destroy. "Al-rameem" means that which has perished and broken into pieces through dryness or age, of trees, leaves, ropes, or bones. From this is His saying: ﴿He says, "Who will give life to the bones while they are crumbled?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78], meaning in the form of ash. A hadith is also narrated: "That wind used to blow upon the people, among whom were the 'Adi and others, and it would snatch the 'Adi from among the people and carry him away."

His saying, ﴿And in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time."﴾ may mean: it was said to them at the beginning of the sending of Salih, peace be upon him: "Believe and obey, and you will enjoy a good provision until your appointed terms," and that is "al-hin" according to this view. This is the saying of al-Hasan, related by him from al-Rummani. His saying, "fa-'ataw" (so they defied), comes after the saying to them, "Enjoy yourselves," in wording within the verse, and in meaning in existence it is later than the saying to them. It may also mean: it was said to them after the slaughter of the she-camel: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days.﴾ [Hud: 65]. And that is "al-hin" according to this interpretation, which is the saying of al-Farra'. His saying, "fa-'ataw," then is not ordered in meaning in existence, because their defiance was before it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves." It is as if the meaning is: their conduct before this statement was defiance, and that was the cause of their being told that and of their punishment.

The majority of reciters read "al-sa'iqa" (الصاعِقَةُ). Al-Kisa'i read, and it is the reading of 'Umar and 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them both, "al-sa'qa" (الصَعْقَةُ). According to both readings it means a great cry, and from it the violent crash of thunder is called "sa'iqa," which is accompanied by fire. A hadith narrates that it is from the "mikhraq" (a rod of flame) in the hand of an angel who drives the clouds. His saying, ﴿while they were looking on﴾, may mean: suddenly, while they saw with their eyes their own state. This is the saying of al-Tabari. It may also mean: while they were looking at that during those three days in which they were informed of it, and saw its signs in the changing of their complexions. This is the saying of Mujahid, according to the order of its explanation earlier. Waiting for the punishment is itself harder than the punishment.
